atoms.b: When the Anglo-Saxons first arrived in Britain, they followed a ((++Pagan party)) religion. In this religion, there were ((++multiple no)) gods who each controlled different aspects of daily life.
The ((++king child)) of the Pagan gods was Woden. He was often shown with his sacred weapon, the spear.
Woden’s wife, Frige, was the goddess of ((++marriage sadness)), childbirth and the home. She was often shown with thread or a spinning wheel.
atoms.sound: Woden’s wife, Freegh, was the goddess of marriage, childbirth and the home. She was often shown with thread or a spinning wheel.

atoms.b: The god of ((++thunder flies)) was called Thunor. He controlled storms and was often seen holding a hammer.
atoms.sound: The god of thunder was called Thunor. He controlled storms and was often seen holding a hammer.

atoms.b: The god of war was Tiw. He was often shown with only one hand after his other hand was bitten off by a ((++wolf ant)).
atoms.sound: The god of war was Tew. He was often shown with only one hand after his other hand was bitten off by a wolf.

instruction.text: The Anglo-Saxons named days of the week after their gods. Match each day to the god it was named after.

instruction.text: Select the picture of a forest.

text: Anglo-Saxon Pagans also believed in elves and dragons. They thought that dragons lived underground and protected treasure like gold and jewels.
hint.label: Did you know?

atoms.a: In the Pagan religion of the Anglo-Saxons, ...
atoms.b: there was a focus on nature.
atoms.sound: In the Pagan religion of the Anglo-Saxons, there was a focus on nature.
Places like forests and hills were seen as sacred

atoms.a: People believed that spirits lived in these places ...
atoms.b: and left offerings for the gods.
atoms.sound: People believed that spirits lived in these places and left offerings for the gods.

feedback.end: As well as leaving offerings in places of nature, Pagans sacrificed animals to ask for good harvests and protection. They also gathered at feasts and festivals to honour their gods.

instruction.text: Drag the items to the grave.

feedback.finish: Anglo-Saxons believed that they took the items they were buried with to the afterlife. Men were often buried with gold and swords, while women were buried with tools for sewing and weaving.
